questions.prompt: What is project quality planning?
options: Inspecting deliverables after they are finished to find defects
Auditing contractors' processes while the work is in progress
Estimating the cost and duration of project activities
Identifying the standards, requirements, procedures, resources and activities needed for deliverables to meet expectations
questions.explanation: Quality planning establishes how quality will be achieved, measured, monitored and maintained throughout the project life cycle.

questions.prompt: When should project quality planning begin?
options: Only after the first deliverables have been produced
Once the project is complete, to record lessons learned
Early in the project life cycle, and be updated when requirements, risks or specifications change
Only when a quality problem has occurred
questions.explanation: Planning provides the foundation for the project, so it starts early. It is not a one-time task and is revised when conditions change.

questions.prompt: What key principle do the notes on quality planning state?
options: Quality should be planned into a project from the beginning rather than inspected in at the end
Quality should be inspected in at the end of each project
Quality planning should wait until the design is complete
Quality is the responsibility of the inspector alone
questions.explanation: Waiting until the end to inspect means defects are found late. Planning aims to prevent them.

questions.prompt: Which of these is an objective of project quality planning?
options: Remove the need for quality control
Prevent defects, errors and rework
Shorten the project by skipping approvals
Transfer all quality risk to the supplier
questions.explanation: Preventing defects, errors and rework is one of the listed objectives. Planning works together with assurance and control rather than replacing them.

questions.prompt: Which tool determines whether quality investments provide sufficient benefits?
options: Benchmarking
Flowcharts
Cost-benefit analysis
Checklists
questions.explanation: Cost-benefit analysis weighs what a quality investment costs against the benefits it gives.

questions.prompt: Which of these is given as an example of a standard to identify in quality planning?
options: ISO 9001
The Pareto principle
The PDCA cycle
A fishbone diagram
questions.explanation: The notes list ISO 9001, building codes, engineering specifications and organisational policies as examples of standards. The others are principles or tools.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a component of a project quality management plan?
options: A list of contractor payment dates
The project's insurance premiums
The client's brand guidelines
Quality policy and objectives
questions.explanation: The plan includes the quality policy and objectives, applicable standards, roles, QA and QC procedures, metrics, acceptance criteria, documentation, non-conformance management and improvement procedures.

questions.prompt: What does expert judgment contribute to quality planning?
options: Statistical evaluation of process variation
Specialist knowledge to establish appropriate quality requirements
A comparison with recognised best practice
A check that planned activities are completed
questions.explanation: Expert judgment draws on specialist knowledge. Statistics, benchmarking and checklists serve other purposes.

questions.prompt: In the construction example, who coordinates quality activities with engineers, contractors, quality inspectors, suppliers and the client?
options: The client alone
The supplier of the materials
The site inspector alone
The project manager
questions.explanation: The project manager coordinates the quality planning activities across all of these parties.

questions.prompt: What do acceptance criteria define?
options: The conditions under which a deliverable is accepted
The procedures for hiring quality staff
The categories of the cost of quality
The order in which project tasks are carried out
questions.explanation: Acceptance criteria, together with measurable indicators, inspection methods and tolerances, state when a deliverable is acceptable.

questions.prompt: Which is one of the five major activities in project quality planning?
options: Close supplier contracts
Record lessons learned after handover
Allocate resources and responsibilities for quality
Approve the final invoice
questions.explanation: The five activities are identifying requirements, establishing standards, planning QA and QC, allocating resources and responsibilities, and defining metrics and acceptance criteria.

questions.prompt: Which component of the quality management plan covers how failures to meet requirements are handled?
options: Quality policy and objectives
Non-conformance management and corrective actions
Roles and responsibilities
Quality metrics and performance indicators
questions.explanation: This component sets out what happens when a deliverable fails to conform, including corrective actions.

questions.prompt: How do flowcharts support quality planning?
options: They estimate the costs of prevention and failure
They compare project practices with best practice
They tick off that required activities were completed
They illustrate processes and help identify possible sources of defects
questions.explanation: Flowcharts show the steps of a process, which makes it easier to see where defects might arise.

questions.prompt: What is the role of checklists in quality planning?
options: They estimate prevention, appraisal and failure costs
They ensure that required quality activities are completed
They evaluate variation using measured data
They supply specialist opinions on requirements
questions.explanation: A checklist makes sure nothing required is missed.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of cause-and-effect diagrams in quality planning?
options: Identifying potential causes of quality problems
Deciding whether quality spending is worthwhile
Estimating prevention and appraisal costs
Setting inspection tolerances for deliverables
questions.explanation: These diagrams help planners think through what might cause a quality problem before it happens.

questions.prompt: How does statistical analysis contribute to quality planning?
options: It sets the quality policy for the organisation
It assigns quality responsibilities to staff
It evaluates variation and process performance using data
It records signed handover documents
questions.explanation: Statistical analysis uses data to judge how much a process varies and how well it performs.

questions.prompt: In the construction example, what is planned for the requirement 'concrete strength'?
options: Specify the concrete mix and conduct strength tests, with results meeting the design specification as evidence
Inspect wiring, earthing and protective devices, with satisfactory test reports as evidence
Conduct regular site inspections, with work conforming to drawings as evidence
Review designs and inspect reinforcement before casting, with approved inspection records as evidence
questions.explanation: Each requirement is paired with a planned activity and acceptance evidence. The other options belong to electrical safety, workmanship and structural safety.

questions.prompt: Which acceptance evidence goes with the requirement 'workmanship'?
options: Satisfactory test and inspection reports
Signed acceptance and handover records
Materials meet approved specifications
Work conforms to drawings and specifications
questions.explanation: Workmanship is planned through regular site inspections, and the evidence is that the work conforms to the drawings and specifications.

questions.prompt: When do quality planning, QA and QC mainly take place?
options: Planning at closure, QA at the start, and QC throughout the project
All three only at project closure
Planning mainly before and during execution, QA throughout the project, and QC during execution and at deliverable milestones
Planning throughout, QA only at the start, and QC only at closure
questions.explanation: This is the typical timing given in the comparison table.

questions.prompt: Which row correctly matches each activity to its main focus?
options: Planning: products and testing; QA: standards and criteria; QC: processes and prevention
Planning: standards, methods, resources and criteria; QA: processes and prevention; QC: products, inspection and testing
Planning: processes and prevention; QA: products and testing; QC: standards and methods
Planning: inspection and testing; QA: standards and resources; QC: prevention
questions.explanation: Planning sets the rules, QA looks at the processes, and QC looks at the products.

questions.prompt: Which set of examples correctly matches quality planning, quality assurance and quality control?
options: Planning: test concrete samples; QA: set concrete strength requirements; QC: audit production procedures
Planning: audit production procedures; QA: test concrete samples; QC: set strength requirements
Planning: test concrete samples; QA: audit production procedures; QC: set strength requirements
Planning: set concrete strength requirements; QA: audit concrete production procedures; QC: test concrete samples
questions.explanation: Setting the requirement is planning, auditing the production procedure is assurance, and testing samples is control.

questions.prompt: What is the main weakness of relying only on inspection at the end of a project?
options: Quality standards do not permit end-of-project inspection
Inspectors are unable to test materials once they are installed
Defects are found only after the work is done, instead of being prevented through planning
End-of-project inspection always costs more than the project budget
questions.explanation: The notes stress that quality should be planned in from the beginning rather than inspected in at the end.

questions.prompt: Midway through a project, the client changes the specification. What do the notes say should happen to the quality plan?
options: It should be updated to reflect the changed requirements
It should stay fixed so the project remains consistent
It should be set aside until the project ends
It should be replaced by a final inspection only
questions.explanation: Quality planning should be updated when project requirements, risks or specifications change.

questions.prompt: A plan sets inspection points before concrete is cast so that errors are corrected before casting. Which benefit of quality planning does this show?
options: Replacing the need for site supervision
Minimising delays caused by rework
Guaranteeing that the client accepts the deliverable
Removing regulatory requirements from the project
questions.explanation: Catching errors before the work is covered or built on reduces rework, and so reduces delay.

questions.prompt: For the requirement 'structural safety', what acceptance evidence is planned?
options: Approved inspection records, after reviewing designs and inspecting reinforcement before casting
Test results that meet the design specification
Signed acceptance and handover records
Materials that meet approved specifications
questions.explanation: The other options are the evidence for concrete strength, completion quality and material quality.

questions.prompt: A final inspection and defect check is planned. Which requirement and acceptance evidence match it?
options: Material quality, with materials meeting approved specifications
Workmanship, with work conforming to drawings
Electrical safety, with satisfactory test reports
Completion quality, with signed acceptance and handover records
questions.explanation: Final inspection and defect checks belong to completion quality, and the evidence is signed acceptance and handover records.

questions.prompt: A draft quality plan lists inspections and tests but names nobody to carry them out and provides no equipment or budget. Which planning activity has been neglected?
options: Establishing quality standards
Allocating resources and responsibilities
Identifying quality requirements
Defining acceptance criteria
questions.explanation: This activity assigns qualified personnel, equipment, budget, testing facilities and responsibilities for quality-related work.

questions.prompt: A planner estimates prevention, appraisal and failure costs to decide how much to spend on quality. Which tool is being used?
options: Benchmarking
Expert judgment
Cost of quality
Statistical analysis
questions.explanation: Cost of quality estimates prevention, appraisal and failure costs.

questions.prompt: Which pairing of tool and purpose is correct?
options: Checklists: estimating prevention, appraisal and failure costs
Flowcharts: comparing project practices with best practice
Cause-and-effect diagrams: ensuring required activities are completed
Benchmarking: comparing project practices with recognised standards or best practices
questions.explanation: Benchmarking compares practice with recognised standards. Checklists ensure activities are completed, flowcharts show processes, and cause-and-effect diagrams find causes.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly compares the main purposes of quality planning, QA and QC?
options: Planning verifies outputs, QA defines requirements, and QC ensures processes are followed
Planning ensures processes are followed, QA verifies outputs, and QC defines requirements
Planning defines requirements and how to meet them, QA ensures processes are suitable and followed, and QC verifies that outputs meet requirements
All three exist only to verify that outputs meet requirements
questions.explanation: Each has a different main purpose, and together they support delivering a project that meets its requirements.
